lectures.title: Cytopenias and Hemochromatosis
lectures.note: Built from the slides only. Prof. Ward's spoken flags (recording, 12 November) lead each note; the stars also mark the slides' own visual emphasis (bold, asterisks, underline, the slide 26 arrow). Prognosis lines come from the guideline-summary slides 104-107. Points the slides state two ways are not keyed one way: the serum iron of anemia of chronic disease (low on slide 13, up or down on slide 27; tell it from iron deficiency by ferritin and total iron-binding capacity), chloroquine as a G6PD trigger (slide 79) or safe (slide 83 table; out loud he sided with the table, so no antimalarial is keyed), where G6PD sits (membrane on slide 79, inside the cell on slide 77), the total iron-binding capacity of anemia of chronic disease (normal or low on slide 13, decreased on slide 27) and thalassemia reticulocytes (a reticulocytosis on slide 13, a low reticulocyte index on slide 87). Beta thalassemia ancestry (slide 86) and the chorionic villus sampling week (slide 92) are not keyed. The slides give no epidemiology for lead poisoning, B12 deficiency or neutropenia.

conditions.name: Iron deficiency anemia
conditions.prof_note: Said: "You guys want to know this slide" (slide 15): microcytosis, hypochromia, low ferritin and saturation, high total iron-binding capacity; replace the iron and still correct the underlying cause. Slide emphasis: chronic blood loss is the most common adult cause; asterisked nail, lip and Plummer-Vinson findings; ferritin is an acute phase reactant; ferrous sulfate and its constipation.

fields.name: Iron deficiency anemia
fields.definition: A microcytic, hypochromic anemia from too little iron; anemia is a reduction in healthy red blood cells or hemoglobin that lowers oxygen delivery to the tissues
fields.etiology: [[★ Chronic blood loss, the most common cause of iron deficiency anemia in adults]] (gastrointestinal loss and menses); dietary factors (vegan diet, tea drinkers, calcium antacids, medications, particularly proton pump inhibitors); malabsorption (gastric bypass surgery, celiac sprue, food allergies); increased demand (pregnancy, growth in infancy or adolescence)
fields.epidemiology: 50% of anemia worldwide; almost 1 million deaths a year, 71% in Africa and Asia, only 1.4% in North America; higher in developing countries. United States: men under 50, 1%; women of childbearing age, 10% (menstrual losses); 9% of children 12 to 36 months are iron deficient and one-third of them develop anemia
fields.risk_factors: Menstruation, gastrointestinal bleeding, vegan diet, tea, calcium antacids, proton pump inhibitors, gastric bypass, celiac sprue, pregnancy, infancy and adolescent growth; low-income families are particularly at risk in the United States
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Fatigue, pallor, decreased exercise tolerance, shortness of breath especially with exertion, smooth tongue, pica (common), [[★ nail bed changes such as koilonychia (spoon-shaped nails), cheilosis, Plummer-Vinson syndrome]]
fields.diagnosis: Complete blood count: microcytosis (mean corpuscular volume below 80 fL), hypochromia (low mean corpuscular hemoglobin). Iron panel: reduced ferritin, reduced transferrin saturation, increased total iron-binding capacity. Smear: microcytic, hypochromic cells. [[★ Ferritin is an acute phase reactant]]: a normal or high ferritin does not exclude iron deficiency; consider an erythrocyte sedimentation rate and/or C-reactive protein. Also urinalysis, fecal occult blood test (stool guaiac), consider prothrombin and partial thromboplastin times. Differential: anemia of chronic disease, thalassemia, lead poisoning, zinc deficiency, sideroblastic anemia
fields.treatment: Treat the underlying cause: oral contraceptive (consider continuous-cycle) for menstrual loss; gastrointestinal bleed: gastroenterology consult for colonoscopy or endoscopy to evaluate for colorectal cancer; stop anticoagulants if anemia is severe (consult cardiology). Iron replacement: [[★ ferrous sulfate]] 325 mg (66 mg elemental iron) once daily or every other day, with at least an as-needed laxative or stool softener for [[★ constipation]]; food lowers side effects and absorption; alternate-day dosing is probably best; or ferrous sulfate 44 mg/5 mL (as elemental iron) once daily in the morning on an empty stomach with a full glass of orange juice. Response: hematocrit halfway to normal in 3 weeks, baseline by 2 months; continue 3 to 6 months after normal values to refill stores. Parenteral iron if intolerant or refractory (most need 1 to 1.5 g). Hematology referral if the diagnosis is not confirmed or there is no response to oral iron
fields.mortality: Almost 1 million deaths a year worldwide. Prognosis: usually resolves once the cause and iron stores are corrected

conditions.name: Anemia of chronic disease
conditions.prof_note: Said: "Want to pay attention to this slide?" (slide 23): interleukin 6 raises hepcidin. Slide emphasis: treat the underlying condition is arrowed as most important; ferritin is an acute phase reactant.

fields.name: Anemia of chronic disease (anemia of chronic inflammation)
fields.definition: Anemia caused by any inflammatory condition; initially resembles iron deficiency anemia
fields.etiology: Any inflammatory condition: infection, autoimmune disease, neoplasm
fields.epidemiology: The second most common anemia; any age; about 1 million people older than 65 in the United States
fields.risk_factors: Older age (more chronic inflammatory disease)
fields.pathology: Multifactorial: inflammatory cytokines, in particular interleukin-6, upregulate hepcidin, which blocks iron absorption; systemic inflammation inhibits renal erythropoietin production; likely direct inflammatory marrow suppression
fields.clinical: Similar to iron deficiency anemia; resembles the causative condition
fields.diagnosis: Same labs as iron deficiency; erythrocyte sedimentation rate and/or C-reactive protein if inflammation is not apparent. Ferritin normal or increased (a ferritin below 30 ng/mL, 67 pmol/L, means coexistent iron deficiency); total iron-binding capacity decreased (slide 27; normal or low on slide 13); reticulocytes usually decreased; mean corpuscular volume normal or low. Serum iron: low on slide 13, up or down on slide 27
fields.treatment: [[★ Treat the underlying condition (most important)]]; may benefit from erythropoietin (epoetin alfa, Procrit); FDA-approved for hemoglobin below 10 g/dL and anemia due to rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease, hepatitis C, zidovudine therapy in HIV, myelosuppressive chemotherapy of solid malignancy, or chronic kidney disease; may need parenteral iron; hematology referral not usually needed
fields.mortality: Prognosis: can persist while the underlying disease is active

fields.name: Sideroblastic anemia
fields.definition: Anemia defined by ring sideroblasts in the bone marrow: iron-containing mitochondria forming a basophilic ring around the nucleus
fields.etiology: Hereditary (usually X-linked); acquired (usually myelodysplastic syndrome); acquired and reversible (alcohol, drugs such as isoniazid and chlorambucil, copper deficiency, hypothermia, lead poisoning). Modern classification: dyserythropoiesis (hypohepcidinemia) or transfusion-dependence (myelodysplastic syndrome, thalassemia)
fields.epidemiology: Rare; about two-thirds of cases present in males in early childhood or adolescence, one-third in young to middle-aged females; can occur at any age
fields.risk_factors: Alcohol, isoniazid, chlorambucil, copper deficiency, hypothermia, lead exposure, myelodysplastic syndrome
fields.pathology: Excess total body iron; iron-laden mitochondria ring the nucleus
fields.clinical: No specific features other than those of anemia; usually moderate, hematocrit 20 to 30%
fields.diagnosis: Variable microcytosis and hypochromia; dimorphic smear (microcytic, normal and macrocytic cells); increased serum iron, transferrin saturation and ferritin; increased zinc if caused by copper deficiency; bone marrow aspirate with ring sideroblasts (the defining feature)
fields.treatment: Remove the offending agent if acquired; red cell transfusion if severe; poor response to recombinant erythropoietin; occasional response to oral pyridoxine (50 to 200 mg/day); luspatercept for myelodysplastic syndrome with ring sideroblasts; hematology referral for diagnostic or transfusion support
fields.mortality: Prognosis: variable; clonal forms may require continued follow-up

fields.name: Lead poisoning (plumbism)
fields.definition: Lead toxicity causing a microcytic, hypochromic anemia
fields.etiology: Industrial exposure, gasoline sniffing, lodged bullets, cooking utensils containing lead, lead-based paint chips, contaminated water (Flint water crisis)
fields.epidemiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.risk_factors: The exposures listed under etiology
fields.pathology: Basophilic stippling: an abnormal collection of nucleic acids in the cells
fields.clinical: Neurologic system most vulnerable: irritability, behavioral changes, peripheral neuropathy. Gastrointestinal: abdominal colic, nausea and constipation, occasionally diarrhea. May be a lead line in the gums
fields.diagnosis: Microcytic, hypochromic anemia with basophilic stippling on the smear; treatment is based on the lead level
fields.treatment: Stop exposure; treatment based on lead level; severe cases with neurologic effects: chelating agents (succimer (Chemet), dimercaprol, ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA))
fields.mortality: Not covered in the lecture

fields.name: Megaloblastic anemia (folate deficiency)
fields.definition: A macrocytic anemia (mean corpuscular volume above 100 fL) with megaloblasts (early red cell precursors), macro-ovalocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils; caused by vitamin B12 or folate deficiency
fields.etiology: Folate: dietary (impoverished, indigent, alcohol use disorder, elderly); increased demand (pregnancy); impaired absorption (proximal small bowel); drugs (methotrexate, 5-fluorouracil, hydroxyurea, phenytoin, metformin)
fields.epidemiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.risk_factors: Poverty, alcohol use disorder, older age, pregnancy, proximal small bowel disease, the drugs listed
fields.pathology: Impaired DNA synthesis causes nuclear-cytoplasmic asynchrony and impaired hematopoiesis; granulocytes and megakaryocytes affected to a lesser degree
fields.clinical: Findings of all anemias: fatigue, pallor, headache; dyspnea and heart failure if severe
fields.diagnosis: Complete blood count: red cells, hemoglobin, hematocrit down; mean corpuscular volume up; mean corpuscular hemoglobin and its concentration normal to slightly up; red cell distribution width up; reticulocytes vary. B12 and folate levels first (not very sensitive), smear; if borderline: homocysteine (needs both B12 and folate) and methylmalonic acid (elevated in B12 deficiency but NOT folate deficiency). Non-megaloblastic macrocytosis (alcohol or drug, hypothyroidism, liver failure, marrow dysplasia) usually stays below 115 fL
fields.treatment: Before replacing folate, evaluate for B12 deficiency (otherwise labs improve but permanent neurologic symptoms may worsen); folic acid 1 mg orally or parenterally daily for 1 to 2 weeks
fields.mortality: Prognosis: counts improve with treatment

conditions.name: Vitamin B12 deficiency and pernicious anemia
conditions.prof_note: Said: "This slide is definitely one that you guys want to pay attention to" (slide 47): methylmalonic acid is for B12 only, not folate. Slide emphasis: pernicious anemia is the most frequent cause; burning of the hands and feet; homocysteine and methylmalonic acid are bold.

fields.name: Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) deficiency; pernicious anemia
fields.definition: Megaloblastic, macrocytic anemia from too little B12; pernicious anemia is the autoimmune form against parietal cells and/or intrinsic factor
fields.etiology: [[★ Pernicious anemia, the most frequent cause of B12 deficiency]]
fields.epidemiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.risk_factors: Not covered in the lecture
fields.pathology: Absorption: peptic digestion frees B12; intrinsic factor from parietal cells binds it and protects it; the complex binds cubilin in the distal ileum; B12 binds transcobalamin and is stored in the liver (about 3 to 4 years or more). Pernicious anemia: autoimmune attack causes gastric mucosal atrophy and increased gastric cancer risk. B12 deficiency demyelinates the dorsal and lateral spinal cord tracts
fields.clinical: Anemia findings (fatigue, pallor, headache; dyspnea and heart failure if severe); glossitis, oral ulcers. Distinguishing: neurologic findings: neuropsychiatric changes (depression, irritability, insomnia, cognitive slowing, dementia); symmetric numbness, tingling, [[★ burning to hands and feet]] (stocking-and-glove distribution); then unsteady gait and loss of position sense; may or may not improve with B12
fields.diagnosis: B12 and folate levels first (not very sensitive) and smear; if borderline: [[★ homocysteine]] (needs both) and [[★ methylmalonic acid]] (elevated in B12 but not folate deficiency). Pernicious anemia: anti-intrinsic factor antibodies (specific, not sensitive); anti-parietal cell antibodies (neither sensitive nor specific); gastric biopsy may show chronic atrophic gastritis; in reality a megaloblastic picture that corrects with B12 is the usual pathway (parenteral B12 trial)
fields.treatment: B12 1000 mcg subcutaneously or intramuscularly weekly for 3 weeks, or oral cobalamin 1000 to 2000 mcg daily; evaluate for B12 deficiency before replacing folate
fields.mortality: Prognosis: counts improve; delayed B12 treatment may leave neurologic deficits; increased risk of gastric cancer in pernicious anemia

fields.name: Anemia of chronic kidney disease (anemia due to renal failure)
fields.definition: A normocytic anemia of chronic kidney disease, primarily from decreased erythropoietin
fields.etiology: Primarily, but not completely, decreased erythropoietin; inflammation and hepcidin restrict available iron
fields.epidemiology: Extremely common in chronic kidney disease; incidence rises as glomerular filtration rate declines; almost universal in dialysis patients
fields.risk_factors: Declining glomerular filtration rate; dialysis
fields.pathology: Inappropriately low erythropoietin response; iron-restricted erythropoiesis
fields.clinical: Not covered in the lecture
fields.diagnosis: Complete blood count: red cells, hemoglobin, hematocrit down; mean corpuscular volume, mean corpuscular hemoglobin and its concentration normal; red cell distribution width up; reticulocytes down. Order complete blood count, reticulocyte count, ferritin and transferrin saturation; assess other causes. A low transferrin saturation may mean iron-restricted erythropoiesis despite a normal or high ferritin
fields.treatment: Correct iron deficiency; consider oral or intravenous iron and an erythropoiesis-stimulating agent based on chronic kidney disease stage, hemoglobin and risk; ferric pyrophosphate citrate (Triferic) in the dialysate replaces the 5 to 7 mg of iron lost each hemodialysis. Follow-up: monitor hemoglobin, iron and blood pressure; nephrology for advanced disease, erythropoiesis-stimulating agent decisions or uncertainty
fields.mortality: Prognosis: often chronic; may improve with iron or an erythropoiesis-stimulating agent

conditions.name: Aplastic anemia
conditions.prof_note: Said: "Be familiar with this slide" (slide 58, treatment).

fields.name: Aplastic anemia
fields.definition: Pancytopenia (loss of red cells, platelets and white cells) with loss of hematopoietic stem cells, the defining feature
fields.etiology: Autoimmune; direct stem cell injury (drugs, chemicals, radiation); viral infections; genetic causes. Drugs and agents: cytotoxic or chemotherapeutic drugs (not aplastic anemia if an expected effect), chloramphenicol, ionizing radiation, toxins (benzene, pesticides). Clonal: paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria, myelodysplastic syndrome, acute myeloid leukemia. Inherited: Fanconi anemia (diagnosed in childhood)
fields.epidemiology: Half of cases in the first three decades, with a small peak in childhood and a second between ages 20 and 25; male-to-female ratio about 1:1; 0.6 to 6.1 cases per million
fields.risk_factors: Chloramphenicol, cytotoxic drugs, ionizing radiation, benzene, pesticides, viral infection, inherited conditions (Fanconi anemia)
fields.pathology: Drugs, chemicals, viruses or mutations can alter the hematopoietic stem cells and predispose them to autoimmune destruction
fields.clinical: Manifestations of pancytopenia: recurrent infections (neutropenia); bleeding, petechiae, purpura (thrombocytopenia); fatigue, pallor
fields.diagnosis: Bone marrow biopsy is required for diagnosis and to exclude other causes
fields.treatment: Urgent or emergent hematology/oncology consultation; bone marrow transplant; infection and bleeding precautions
fields.mortality: Five-year survival above 75% after bone marrow transplant from a suitable donor; most untreated patients die within one year from complications. Prognosis depends on severity and response to treatment

fields.name: Leukopenia and neutropenia
fields.definition: Leukopenia is a low total white blood cell count; neutropenia is defined by the absolute neutrophil count
fields.etiology: Viral illness, medications or chemotherapy, autoimmune disease, nutrient deficits, marrow pathology
fields.epidemiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.risk_factors: Infection risk rises with severity, duration and impaired immune status
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Profound neutropenia may have subtle findings; fever with an absolute neutrophil count below 500 is an emergency
fields.diagnosis: Absolute neutrophil count = white count x (neutrophils + bands)% / 100. Mild 1,000 to 1,500; moderate 500 to 999; severe below 500 cells/microliter. Repeat complete blood count with differential, review the trend and smear, check other cell lines. Escalate to hematology for persistent or unexplained severe neutropenia, other cytopenias or an abnormal smear
fields.treatment: Fever with an absolute neutrophil count below 500 (or expected to fall below 500): prompt assessment, vitals, targeted examination, cultures, empiric antipseudomonal antibiotics without delay. Chronic: stop an offending drug, correct deficiencies, granulocyte colony-stimulating factor for selected patients. Education: report fever or rigors promptly; monitor counts
fields.mortality: Prognosis: transient viral leukopenia often resolves after recovery; persistent or severe neutropenia carries greater infection risk and may indicate marrow disease

conditions.name: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia
conditions.prof_note: Slide emphasis: autoimmune hemolytic anemia carries an increased risk of venous thromboembolism (bold); hemolysis labs bilirubin, haptoglobin, lactate dehydrogenase, schistocytes and jaundice are bold.

fields.name: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia
fields.definition: Hemolytic anemia (shortened red cell survival from premature destruction) caused by antibody against the red cell membrane
fields.etiology: Primary (de novo antibody production; almost always IgG) or secondary: viruses (human immunodeficiency virus, hepatitis, Epstein-Barr virus, SARS-CoV-2); autoimmune disorders (lupus, rheumatoid arthritis, scleroderma, ulcerative colitis); lymphoproliferative disorders (leukemia, lymphoma, multiple myeloma); pregnancy. Transfusion reaction is also immune-mediated
fields.epidemiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.risk_factors: The secondary causes listed
fields.pathology: Extracorpuscular, immune-mediated hemolysis; hemolytic anemias share a shorter red cell life span, compensatory erythropoiesis (marrow hyperplasia, reticulocytosis) and retention of breakdown products
fields.clinical: Anemia symptoms (fatigue, shortness of breath, chest pain, pallor; severe: high-output heart failure, shock); differentiating: [[★ jaundice]], splenomegaly, joint pain, hematuria; [[★ increased risk of venous thromboembolism]]
fields.diagnosis: Hemolysis labs: complete blood count, reticulocyte count, [[★ bilirubin]] (unconjugated greater than conjugated; jaundice above 2.0 mg/dL), [[★ lactate dehydrogenase]] up, [[★ haptoglobin]] decreased or absent (intravascular), urinalysis, smear ([[★ schistocytes]]). Direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test: positive when the washed red cells carry IgG or complement. Consider D-dimer and bilateral leg ultrasound for deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism
fields.treatment: Consider immediate stabilization if hemoglobin below 6, a rapid decline, or instability; contact the blood bank. Rule out secondary causes. Glucocorticoids initially (e.g., prednisone 60 to 100 mg daily); rituximab (anti-CD20); other: immunosuppressants, splenectomy. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis for inpatients, consider for outpatients
fields.mortality: Prognosis: relapse may occur; outcome depends on cause and response

conditions.name: G6PD deficiency
conditions.prof_note: Said: "Be familiar with Heinz bodies, what they are, what they represent" (slides 77-78); hemolysis is intravascular and extravascular. Slide emphasis: fava beans and acute hemolytic anemia are bold. Antimalarials: slide 79 lists chloroquine as a trigger, the slide 83 table as safe, and he said "don't just assume all anti-malarial medications carry that same risk", so no antimalarial is keyed.

fields.name: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency
fields.definition: The most common genetic disorder of erythrocytes: an enzyme deficiency that leaves red cells open to oxidative damage, causing [[★ acute hemolytic anemia]] on oxidative stress
fields.etiology: X-linked recessive. Common triggers: [[★ fava beans]], naphthalene (mothballs), antimalarials (some; Prof. Ward said chloroquine does not carry the same risk), nitrofurantoin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (Bactrim), methylene blue, phenazopyridine, quinolones
fields.epidemiology: 200 to 400 million people. Prevalence: Kurdish Jews 60 to 70%; Sardinians 4 to 35%; Nigerians 22%; Thai people 17%; American Black people 11 to 12%; Brazilian Black people 8%; Greeks 6%; South China about 6%; India 3%; Japanese and Koreans 0 to 1%
fields.risk_factors: Male sex (X-linked recessive; carrier females have two red cell populations and are generally unaffected); exposure to the oxidant triggers
fields.pathology: G6PD is needed in the glutathione pathway; without reduced glutathione, oxidative stress forms Heinz bodies inside the red cell; splenic macrophages remove them by taking a chunk of the cell (bite cells); intravascular and extravascular hemolysis
fields.clinical: No symptoms until oxidative stress; drug-induced hemolysis is acute, of variable severity, after a lag of 2 to 3 days: abdominal pain, jaundice, dark urine, splenomegaly
fields.diagnosis: Labs consistent with hemolytic anemia; during an attack the smear may show Heinz bodies and bite cells; confirmed by a low G6PD level roughly 8 weeks after an attack
fields.treatment: Avoid the trigger ("don't eat that"); hydrate; transfuse if needed; splenectomy only for recurrent attacks. Education: avoid oxidative triggers; seek care for jaundice or dark urine
fields.mortality: Prognosis: usually favorable with trigger avoidance

conditions.name: Thalassemia
conditions.prof_note: Said: "Did I tell you guys to pay attention to slide 88?" (thalassemia labs). Slide emphasis: the globin imbalance line is bold; iron overload is bold and underlined.

fields.name: Thalassemia (alpha and beta)
fields.definition: A hemoglobinopathy from mutations causing deficient synthesis of alpha or beta globins
fields.etiology: Inherited mutations of the globin genes (4 alpha, 2 beta); the phenotype depends on how many are mutated, from silent carrier (one alpha gene lost) to incompatible with life
fields.epidemiology: Alpha thalassemia: Southern China, Malaysia, Thailand, Mediterranean region; mild forms in African origin. Asian ancestry often has the alpha thalassemia 1 trait (both deletions on one side, higher risk of hydrops fetalis); African ancestry more often the alpha thalassemia 2 trait (one deletion on each side)
fields.risk_factors: Family history (preconception testing and counseling available)
fields.pathology: [[★ Imbalance in expression leads to accumulation and precipitation of globin subunits]], causing red cell destruction in the spleen; most erythroblasts die in the marrow
fields.clinical: Variable by mutation: hemolytic anemia, [[★ iron overload]], splenomegaly, extramedullary hematopoiesis, jaundice, skeletal changes
fields.diagnosis: Generally low hemoglobin, mean corpuscular volume, mean corpuscular hemoglobin and reticulocyte index (marrow failure); Coombs negative (slide 87); slide 13 adds more microcytosis for the hemoglobin level with a normal or high red cell count, and a reticulocytosis, against the low reticulocyte index of slide 87. Complete blood count, iron studies, reticulocyte count; hemoglobin electrophoresis; gene testing
fields.treatment: Supportive: transfusion when absolutely necessary (can worsen iron overload); folic acid; genetic counseling. Hematology for severe forms; iron monitoring
fields.mortality: Prognosis: trait often mild; severe forms need lifelong monitoring; the most severe genotype is incompatible with life

conditions.name: Sickle cell anemia
conditions.prof_note: Said: "A chest x-ray is the first imaging study if you're suspecting acute chest syndrome" (slide 94); "Be familiar with the management here" (slide 98).

fields.name: Sickle cell anemia (sickle cell disease)
fields.definition: A hemoglobinopathy in which hemoglobin S (two alpha and two mutant beta globins) polymerizes under low oxygen tension and forms a sickle shape
fields.etiology: Mutation of a beta globin gene
fields.epidemiology: Distribution follows the malaria belt; heterozygous carriers (HbAS) are 90% less likely to have severe malaria
fields.risk_factors: Parents carrying the mutation (preconception screening); reactive lung disease increases the risk of acute chest syndrome
fields.pathology: Polymerized HbS sickles red cells, causing microvascular occlusion and infarction of any tissue with vascular beds; symptoms begin around 5 months of age as fetal hemoglobin gives way to HbS; fetal hemoglobin of 10 to 20% seems to lessen severity
fields.clinical: Anemia almost universal (hematocrit 15 to 30%); pain crisis (acute pain, tenderness, anxiety, tachycardia); splenic infarct, aseptic necrosis of the femoral or humeral heads, retinopathy, kidney disease; leg ulcers; pediatric stroke (300 times unaffected children; 25% have a stroke by 45); priapism; susceptibility to encapsulated bacteria. Infants: failure to thrive, pain, anemia, splenomegaly, chronic infections, swelling of the extremities. Acute chest syndrome: chest pain, fever, shortness of breath, hypoxemia, new infiltrates on chest X-ray
fields.diagnosis: Four screening periods: preconception, prenatal (chorionic villus sampling), neonatal (all 50 states; missed cases usually present within two years), post-natal
fields.treatment: Hydroxyurea raises fetal hemoglobin and reduces vaso-occlusive events; vaccinations, indicated childhood penicillin prophylaxis, infection education; urgent assessment for fever, chest pain or hypoxemia, new neurologic deficit; transfusion or exchange for selected severe events (watch alloimmunization and iron loading); hematology follow-up, organ surveillance, consideration of curative therapies
fields.mortality: Acute chest syndrome is the leading cause of death, with more than 10% mortality in adults. Prognosis: lifelong disease; prevention reduces complications

conditions.name: Hemoglobin C and hemoglobin SC disease

fields.name: Hemoglobin C; hemoglobin SC disease (sickle cell SC)
fields.definition: Hemoglobin C comes from a different beta globin mutation and does not polymerize; hemoglobin SC disease combines one beta-C with one beta-S globin
fields.etiology: A different mutation in the beta globin gene; SC = inheriting the C and the S mutations
fields.epidemiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.risk_factors: Not covered in the lecture
fields.pathology: HbC does not polymerize
fields.clinical: Hemoglobin SC disease generally has a course between sickle cell anemia and sickle cell trait
fields.diagnosis: Not covered in the lecture
fields.treatment: Not covered in the lecture
fields.mortality: Not covered in the lecture

conditions.name: Hemochromatosis (primary and secondary)
conditions.prof_note: Said: "Be familiar with treatments here" (slide 104): therapeutic phlebotomy; and the lifespan slide 105.

fields.name: Hemochromatosis (iron overload), primary and secondary
fields.definition: Excess iron deposition throughout the body
fields.etiology: Primary: autosomal recessive mutation of genes that control iron absorption. Secondary: excessive iron supplementation, chronic liver disease, anemia (parenteral iron overload; transfusion-related overload in children)
fields.epidemiology: HFE hemochromatosis usually presents in adults
fields.risk_factors: Family history (first-degree relatives); iron supplements and excessive alcohol
fields.pathology: Iron deposition raises oxidative stress, causing fibrosis and organ dysfunction; liver, heart, joints, endocrine organs and skin most affected; pituitary iron causes hypogonadotropic hypogonadism
fields.clinical: Asymptomatic early; fatigue; skin bronzing (face, neck, groin, extensor forearms and lower legs); joint pain, especially the second and third metacarpophalangeal joints and knees; cardiomyopathy, chest pain, dyspnea on exertion; decreased libido, impotence, amenorrhea, small testes, gynecomastia, reduced body hair
fields.diagnosis: Iron panel: ferritin below 300 micrograms/L and transferrin saturation below 45% means no iron overload (ferritin is an acute phase reactant: read the whole picture). Liver biopsy with Prussian blue: primary shows hepatic iron sparing the Kupffer cells until later; secondary (parenteral overload) shows iron predominantly in Kupffer cells. Consider HFE testing with elevated transferrin saturation or ferritin; offer first-degree relative screening
fields.treatment: Primary: therapeutic phlebotomy with ferritin-guided follow-up. Secondary: treat the cause; consider chelation when phlebotomy is unsuitable. Avoid iron supplements and excessive alcohol; individualize dietary advice
fields.mortality: Early treatment can prevent organ damage; assess fibrosis and monitor cirrhosis for liver cancer; established cirrhosis may persist

lectures.title: Hematologic Malignancies Part I
lectures.note: Built from the slides only. Prof. Gannon's spoken flags (recording, 18 November) lead each note; the stars also mark the slides' own visual emphasis (bold, underline). The deck splits the syllabus differently: this lecture teaches ALL and AML (syllabus Hematological Malignancies 1) and MDS, the myeloproliferative neoplasms and CML (syllabus Hematologic Malignancies II); lymphoma, CLL and myeloma are Lecture 50, and secondary polycythemia is on neither deck. Points the slides state two ways are not keyed one way: "the most common leukemia" (AML on slide 31, CLL in Lecture 50, CML 15-20% on slide 58), the ALL ages (under 15 and peak ~50 on slide 18; under 5 and over 50 on slide 21), children's and adults' ALL survival (>90% vs ~90%; ~30-40% vs ~40%), and the wording for stopping TKIs (major molecular response on slide 63, remission on slide 66). Spoken numbers that differ from the slides (chronic phase "five to 6%" blasts, blast phase ">20%", stopping after 3 or 5 years) are not used; the slides' are. The joke protocol slides 26 and 39 are excluded. The slides give no diagnostics for myelofibrosis and no epidemiology for the MPNs beyond "rare".

conditions.name: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL)
conditions.prof_note: Said: "Remember that ALL is associated with this BCR-ABL mutation ... chromosome nine and 22. Write it down" (slide 20); "remember ALL in children and then older adults" (bimodal, slide 18); "20% or greater blast in the bone marrow" (slide 25); the lumbar puncture is "the big one" because CNS leukemia is common in ALL. Slide emphasis: most common malignancy under 15 (underlined); flow cytometry and bone marrow biopsy (underlined); Ph+ ALL = TKI + chemotherapy (bold).

fields.name: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL)
fields.definition: A leukemia originating with the lymphoid progenitor/stem cells: very immature cells with a rapid ability to proliferate; [[★ defined by blast cells of lymphoid origin >= 20% in bone marrow]]
fields.etiology: Mutagenesis at the lymphoblast stage, at various stages of differentiation into B or T lymphocytes. Children: often excess chromosome copies (hyperdiploidy, favorable prognosis). Adults: [[★ the most common mutation is BCR-ABL, from translocation of chromosomes 9 and 22 (the Philadelphia chromosome)]]. One-third of adult and pediatric patients have no chromosome abnormalities (need mutation analysis; relatively favorable)
fields.epidemiology: [[★ Bimodal distribution]]: the most common malignancy under the age of 15 (United States 5-year survival >90%); adult peak incidence around 50 years of age. Slide 21: children under 5 and adults over age 50; male gender
fields.risk_factors: Radiation exposure (prior radiation for cancer treatment; atomic bomb exposure in Japan); chemical exposures (benzene, certain chemotherapies); viral infections (EBV (Epstein-Barr virus), HTLV-1 (human T-lymphotropic virus type 1), Caribbean countries); genetic syndromes (Down syndrome, Fanconi anemia, others; ?family history); age (children under 5, adults over 50); male gender
fields.pathology: B-cell precursor ALL often presents in a leukemic phase (primarily blasts and marrow involvement); T-cell ALL is rarer, usually with lymphoma-like characteristics, and may involve the thymus; subtype lymphoblastic lymphoma (immature, aggressive, more lymphoma features). Often diffuse marrow and peripheral blood involvement, in contrast to aggressive lymphomas (nodal or extranodal, minimal marrow)
fields.clinical: Symptoms of excessive blast production and lymphoid (nodal) characteristics. Anemia: fatigue, weakness, lightheadedness, shortness of breath, pale skin. Thrombocytopenia: bruising (often petechiae or purpura), bleeding. Ineffective white cells: infections. [[★ B-symptoms: weight loss, fever, night sweats]], loss of appetite. >50% present with lymphadenopathy, hepatomegaly or splenomegaly. Bone or joint pain from excessive marrow production. Mediastinal mass on chest X-ray in T-cell ALL
fields.diagnosis: Labs: anemia, thrombocytopenia, leukopenia or marked leukocytosis (white count often > 30K; 30% with neutropenia). Confirmed by [[★ flow cytometry and bone marrow biopsy]]: flow identifies the markers and B-cell or T-cell nature; biopsy shows marrow infiltration and allows chromosome and mutation testing. Also imaging, counts, electrolytes, coagulation and [[★ lumbar puncture]] (central nervous system (CNS) involvement is an adverse risk factor). [[★ Lymphoid blasts >= 20% in bone marrow]]. Cytogenetics and mutation analyses for prognosis. Differential: acute myeloid leukemia (AML); chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), aggressive lymphomas; hairy cell leukemia; lymphoblastic lymphoma (hard to tell apart, treated similarly); atypical lymphocytosis of mononucleosis or pertussis (flow cytometry shows ALL is clonal)
fields.treatment: Philadelphia chromosome-negative: pediatric-like regimens usually for patients < 40 (intensive chemotherapy with induction, consolidation and maintenance; chemotherapy, steroids, often targeted agents); older adults may need therapy changes and dose adjustments. [[★ Philadelphia chromosome-positive: tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI) + chemotherapy]]. Allogeneic stem cell transplant where feasible for adverse risk or relapsed ALL. Referral to and management by a hematologist/oncologist (ideally an ALL specialist); most are admitted for work-up and treatment; frequent follow-up and life-long surveillance; clinical trials where feasible
fields.mortality: Often positive, particularly for children: five-year overall survival ~90% under 15, with intensive chemotherapy for 2-5 years. Adults: five-year overall survival historically ~40%, cure rate decreasing with age (outcomes poor over 40); improving with immunotherapies. central nervous system involvement is an adverse risk factor

conditions.name: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML)
conditions.prof_note: Said: "Highlight, star, underline ... Auer rods ... pathognomonic for AML" (slides 31, 36); "20% blast in your bone marrow" (slide 38); bone marrow biopsy and flow cytometry are "your backbone testing" (slide 36). Played down: the FAB table (slide 33) and the secondary-AML subgroup modifiers (slide 38). Slide emphasis: Auer rods confirm myeloid etiology (underlined); secondary AML poor outcome, gum involvement, fit vs unfit therapy, allogeneic transplant IF remission (bold).

fields.name: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML)
fields.definition: A leukemia originating with the myeloid progenitor/stem cells: very immature cells with a rapid ability to proliferate; [[★ Auer rods are pathognomonic]]; defined by myeloid blasts >= 20% (certain genetic mutations: 10% or higher)
fields.etiology: Multiple subtypes by initial mutation and stage of maturation; tremendous cytogenetic and mutational variety, so risk is favorable, intermediate or poor. Secondary AML: arising from another myeloid neoplasm (myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS), myeloproliferative neoplasm (MPN), others) or after treatment of another cancer, with poor outcomes. Historically ~8 FAB subtypes (M0-M7), now 18 by WHO
fields.epidemiology: Mostly adults, particularly older adults (>60 years old); unusual in children outside of neonates; male gender
fields.risk_factors: Prior high-dose radiation; benzene, petroleum, certain chemotherapies (alkylators); HIV; Down syndrome, Fanconi anemia, others, ?family history; age over 60; male gender; prior MDS or MPN; prior cancer therapy
fields.pathology: FAB: M0 undifferentiated, M1 minimal maturation, M2 with maturation, M3 acute promyelocytic (APL), M4 acute myelomonocytic, M5 acute monocytic, M6 acute erythroid, M7 acute megakaryocytic. M4 and M5 tend to have more extramedullary involvement; erythroid and megakaryocytic leukemias are very rare. Auer rods are fused lysosomes
fields.clinical: Symptoms of excess blast production, immune dysfunction and infections. Anemia: fatigue, weakness, lightheadedness, shortness of breath, pale skin. Thrombocytopenia: bruising (often petechiae or purpura), bleeding. Infections. B-symptoms: weight loss, fever, night sweats. Myelomonocytic and monocytic subtypes may have gum involvement (hyperplasia) or extramedullary disease
fields.diagnosis: Labs: anemia, thrombocytopenia, white count often elevated but may be low; unlike ALL, > 200K is rare, and all > 100K need emergent leukapheresis. Confirmed by [[★ flow cytometry and bone marrow biopsy]] (flow differentiates it from ALL); [[★ morphology showing Auer rods confirms myeloid etiology]]; counts, electrolytes, coagulation, mutation sequencing, lumbar puncture. [[★ Myeloid blasts >= 20%]] (10% or higher with certain genetic mutations); cytogenetics and mutations for prognosis; AML with prior MDS or MPN and therapy-related AML = secondary AML. Differential: ALL, CML, MDS, myeloproliferative disorders; pancytopenia of infection, aplastic anemia, nutritional deficiency, drugs (flow shows AML is clonal)
fields.treatment: Fit patients: intensive chemotherapy, often cytarabine + anthracycline (7+3). Unfit patients: low-intensity therapy, frequently hypomethylating agents +/- a BCL-2 inhibitor (venetoclax). Allogeneic stem cell transplant for most intermediate- and high-risk patients IF able to achieve remission. Referral to and management by a hematologist/oncologist (ideally a leukemia specialist); admission for work-up and treatment; life-long surveillance; clinical trials
fields.mortality: Frequent relapse and high treatment-related mortality; overall 48% alive at 1 year, about 25-30% at 5 years; highest for favorable risk (about 2/3 at 5 years) and younger patients; over 70 only 5% at 5 years; adverse risk or secondary AML about 10%

conditions.name: Acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL)
conditions.prof_note: Said: "The thing I want you to remember about APL, bleeding, DIC, coagulopathy, and that it does not need chemotherapy. ATRA and arsenic are the treatments for APL" (slide 43). Slide emphasis: DIC and bleeding, arsenic trioxide and ATRA, >90% cure (bold). PML-RARA was not said aloud.

fields.name: Acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL)
fields.definition: A rare AML subtype (FAB M3) caused by arrested differentiation at the promyelocyte
fields.etiology: Translocation of chromosomes 15 and 17, fusing the PML-RARA genes
fields.epidemiology: Rare AML subtype; otherwise not covered in the lecture
fields.risk_factors: Not covered in the lecture
fields.pathology: Arrested differentiation at the promyelocyte; t(15;17) PML-RARA fusion
fields.clinical: [[★ Frequently presents with emergent complications, including DIC (disseminated intravascular coagulation) and bleeding]]
fields.diagnosis: The AML work-up (flow cytometry, bone marrow biopsy, coagulation); t(15;17) PML-RARA
fields.treatment: [[★ Unique treatment approach: arsenic trioxide and all-trans-retinoic acid (ATRA)]]
fields.mortality: High early mortality; if the initial presentation is survived, excellent prognosis (>90% cure rate)

conditions.name: Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS)
conditions.prof_note: Said: the blast drill on slide 47 ("If it's 10%, is it leukemia? No. If it's 15%, leukemia? No."; 20% = leukemia). Slide emphasis: defined by dysplasia; cytopenias, frequently anemia; low risk defined by anemia; more common in men; low risk + anemia = erythropoiesis-stimulating agents; the only cure is allogeneic transplant (bold).

fields.name: Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS)
fields.definition: A group of myeloid malignancies defined by dysplasia (abnormal appearing) of myeloid cells, distorting hematopoiesis, with immune dysregulation and genomic changes (mutations)
fields.etiology: Often evolves from milder abnormal stem cell clones (clonal hematopoiesis) until the dysplasia of MDS develops; often idiopathic; sometimes prior chemotherapy or radiation
fields.epidemiology: Older population (median 70 years); more common in men
fields.risk_factors: Older age; male sex; prior chemotherapy or radiation; often idiopathic
fields.pathology: Typically a hypercellular marrow, but the cells are not functional. Low risk MDS is commonly defined by anemia with a low risk of AML progression; very high-risk MDS has elevated blasts and substantial overlap with AML
fields.clinical: Many are asymptomatic and found incidentally. Fatigue, weakness, pale skin from anemia; infections from ineffective white cells; bleeding from thrombocytopenia
fields.diagnosis: Most frequently anemia; neutropenia; occasional thrombocytopenia; neutrophils with morphological abnormalities; often red cell abnormalities (multinucleated or hyperplastic); [[★ higher risk MDS may have blasts but < 20% (otherwise AML)]]
fields.treatment: Highly dependent on blood counts, risk status and mutations. [[★ Low risk + anemia: erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (ESA)]] and red cell transfusions as needed; neutropenia: myeloid growth factors (careful not to overstimulate blasts); higher risk: chemotherapy or hypomethylating agents; [[★ the only curative therapy is allogeneic stem cell transplant]], but high risk and a limited role
fields.mortality: Highly variable by risk: lower risk median survival > 5 years with very low risk of AML; very high risk median overall survival 9 months and > 80% risk of AML within 5 years. Low risk patients often have complications from anemia, bleeding and/or infections; the goal of treatment is quality of life. Prior MDS makes AML secondary (poor outcome)

conditions.name: Polycythemia vera
conditions.prof_note: Said: "Polycythemia vera, JAK2 mutation, you may come across this on your testing, you might wanna remember that or write that down" (slide 52). Slide emphasis: classic pruritus with warm baths or showers (bold). Not said aloud: the 14-year survival, ~5% transformation, smoking cessation. Secondary polycythemia (a syllabus item) is not on the deck.

fields.name: Polycythemia vera
fields.definition: A myeloproliferative neoplasm (a rare myeloid malignancy with atypical proliferation of mature cell lines): over-production of red blood cells, increasing blood viscosity
fields.etiology: [[★ Commonly the result of a JAK2 mutation]]
fields.epidemiology: Myeloproliferative neoplasms are rare; otherwise not covered in the lecture
fields.risk_factors: JAK2 mutation; otherwise not covered in the lecture
fields.pathology: Over-production of red blood cells (increased blood viscosity)
fields.clinical: Usually non-specific: fatigue, headaches, blurry vision. [[★ Classic: pruritus with warm baths or showers]]
fields.diagnosis: JAK2 mutation; otherwise not covered in the lecture
fields.treatment: Phlebotomy, hydroxyurea; refer to a hematologist; advise to stop smoking
fields.mortality: Complications: thrombosis, splenomegaly, bleeding. Prognosis excellent: estimated survival of 14 years; leukemic transformation rare (~5% of cases)

fields.name: Myelofibrosis
fields.definition: A myeloproliferative neoplasm: over-production of mature myeloid cell lines, eventually causing fibrosis of the marrow; the most aggressive of the MPNs
fields.etiology: Abnormal JAK-STAT pathway mutations, causing elevated cytokines and marked excess proliferation of all myeloid cell lines
fields.epidemiology: Myeloproliferative neoplasms are rare; otherwise not covered in the lecture
fields.risk_factors: JAK-STAT pathway mutations; otherwise not covered in the lecture
fields.pathology: Elevated cytokines, excess proliferation of all myeloid cell lines, then fibrosis of the marrow
fields.clinical: Usually non-specific: fatigue and abdominal symptoms from splenomegaly (pain, early satiety and/or bloating); night sweats, fever, weight loss also common
fields.diagnosis: Not covered in the lecture
fields.treatment: Often targeted inhibitors (JAK inhibitors), which are palliative; refer to a hematologist upon diagnosis
fields.mortality: Complications: severe splenomegaly, portal hypertension, bleeding, progression to secondary AML. Prognosis highly variable: low risk can live 10-15 years; high risk often survive less than 2 years

fields.name: Essential thrombocythemia
fields.definition: A myeloproliferative neoplasm: over-production of platelets
fields.etiology: Often gene mutations in the JAK-STAT pathway, causing overproduction of platelets; rarely inherited
fields.epidemiology: Myeloproliferative neoplasms are rare; otherwise not covered in the lecture
fields.risk_factors: JAK-STAT pathway gene mutations; rarely inherited
fields.pathology: Bleeding despite high platelets can occur from acquired von Willebrand factor deficiency (a shortage of the factor at the site of injury)
fields.clinical: Mostly asymptomatic, but may present with clotting (headaches, fatigue, paresthesias or vision changes) or bleeding
fields.diagnosis: High platelets; otherwise not covered in the lecture
fields.treatment: [[★ Aspirin, hydroxyurea]], or other agents to reduce clotting risk; refer to a hematologist; advise to stop smoking
fields.mortality: Complications: clotting, including CVA (stroke) and MI (myocardial infarction). Prognosis excellent: generally a normal life span with appropriate management

conditions.name: Chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML)
conditions.prof_note: Said: she walked through the slide 64 milestones (optimal BCR-ABL1 under 10% at 3 months, under 1% at 6, under 0.1% at 12) and shows the table to nearly every patient. Not taught aloud: the slide 61 differential. Slide emphasis: BCR-ABL / Philadelphia chromosome and "now largely a chronic disorder" (bold); splenomegaly and bone marrow biopsy + PCR for BCR-ABL1 (underlined); the phases and tyrosine kinase inhibitors (bold). Out loud she called chronic phase "five to 6% blast" (slide: <5%).

fields.name: Chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML)
fields.definition: A leukemia originating from hematopoietic stem cells that produces increased numbers of granulocytes (more mature than blasts); historically progressed from a chronic condition to acute leukemia in ~4-6 years
fields.etiology: [[★ Hallmark BCR-ABL mutation from fusion of chromosomes 22 and 9: the Philadelphia chromosome]]. The translocation attaches the BCR gene to the ABL1 gene; the BCR-ABL fusion protein is a functional enzyme that promotes cell proliferation and reduces apoptosis (the cell "can't turn off" and constantly divides)
fields.epidemiology: 15-20% of all leukemias; median age 45-55 years; either sex, slightly more common in men
fields.risk_factors: May be more common in radiation bomb victims (Japan); no other identified risk factors
fields.pathology: Marrow: marked granulocytic proliferation and myelocytes in chronic phase. Phases: chronic (stable), early proliferative, no or few blasts (<5%), 85-90% of presentations, excellent prognosis; accelerated, often 10-19% blasts, dysplastic granulocytes and fibrosis, significant splenomegaly, ~4-5%; blast phase/crisis, behaves as an acute leukemia (usually AML-like), unique chromosomal and mutational abnormalities, ~1-2%
fields.clinical: ~50% asymptomatic at diagnosis (found from leukocytosis on a complete blood count). Anemia: fatigue, weakness, lightheadedness, shortness of breath. [[★ Abdominal swelling or discomfort from splenomegaly]]. B-symptoms: weight loss, fever, night sweats, loss of appetite
fields.diagnosis: Labs: [[★ marked leukocytosis, thrombocytosis]], anemia; white count often > 100K and up to 500K; platelets usually elevated; very low blasts unless accelerated or blast phase. [[★ Confirmed by bone marrow biopsy and PCR for the BCR-ABL1 mutation]]: PCR in a patient with marked granulocytosis confirms the diagnosis and monitors treatment response; flow cytometry for lineage and mutation analysis. Differential: other myeloproliferative disorders, namely myelofibrosis (the slide also names CMML, never expanded): in CML red cell morphology is normal and the hematocrit is not elevated; definitive when BCR/ABL1 is positive on PCR. Reactive leukocytosis of infection: no splenomegaly, white count usually < 50K, BCR/ABL1 negative
fields.treatment: [[★ Tyrosine kinase inhibitors are the hallmark of therapy for chronic phase CML]] (6 approved agents). Milestones (BCR-ABL1): optimal < 10% at 3 months, < 1% at 6 months, < 0.1% at 12 and > 18 months; warning > 10% at 3 months, 1-10% at 6, 0.1-1% at 12 and > 18; failure > 10% at 6 months, > 1% at 12 and > 18; < 0.01% after 18 months = treatment-free remission range. Major molecular response for 2 years may allow stopping (recurrence in 50%; most recapture deep responses). Advanced CML (accelerated or blast phase) has different considerations; blast phase needs AML-like regimens (poor responses to TKIs). Allogeneic stem cell transplant for young healthy patients with TKI resistance or advanced stage. Referral to and management by a hematologist; treatment for life unless sustained major molecular remission x 2 years; clinical trials for advanced phase
fields.mortality: Once fatal; [[★ now largely a chronic disorder: most patients live normal lives on TKIs]] or stay off therapy after sustained major molecular response. Accelerated or blast phase outcomes remain poor (median survival < 12 months)

lectures.note: Built from the slides only. Ms. Gannon's spoken flags (recording, 18 November, parts 3-4) lead each note; the stars also mark the slides' own bold and underline. The slides give no epidemiology for MGUS or smoldering myeloma and no treatment for MGUS, mantle cell or marginal zone lymphoma beyond the general non-Hodgkin lines.

conditions.name: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (small lymphocytic lymphoma)
conditions.prof_note: Said: "High white count, painless lymphadenopathy, underline, underline, star, star"; flow cytometry is the most important work-up, CD19 + CD5 pathognomonic so no marrow biopsy; Richter transformation "you should highlight"; an isolated white count alone does not equal treatment. Slide emphasis: mature B cells, asymptomatic on routine labs, lymphocytosis >5K, watch and wait.

fields.name: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (small lymphocytic lymphoma)
fields.definition: A proliferative leukemia of [[★ mature B-cell lymphocytes in blood, bone marrow, lymph nodes, and spleen]]; called small lymphocytic lymphoma in the nodes. Rare mature T-cell leukemias are T-cell prolymphocytic leukemia
fields.etiology: Mutagenesis in mature B cells gives a clonal population; 80% of cases come from loss or addition of chromosomal material in one of four abnormalities: [[★ deletion 13q, deletion 11q, trisomy 12, deletion 17p]]
fields.epidemiology: 1% of all new cancer cases in the United States; median age at diagnosis 70 years; twice as common in males; more common in Eastern Europeans and those of Jewish descent
fields.risk_factors: Age (median onset 70); male sex; Eastern European or Jewish descent; no known occupational or environmental risk factors
fields.pathology: A clone of mature B cells coexpressing [[★ CD19 and CD5]] accumulates in blood, marrow, nodes and spleen; ineffective white cells cause infections, marrow crowding causes anemia and thrombocytopenia
fields.clinical: [[★ Frequently diagnosed while asymptomatic]] on routine blood work; [[★ painless lymphadenopathy (50-90%)]], localized or generalized, firm, mobile; B symptoms (weight loss, night sweats, fevers) in 5-10%; anemia: fatigue; thrombocytopenia: easy bruising, bleeding; infections; splenomegaly (~40%), less commonly hepatomegaly
fields.diagnosis: [[★ Lymphocytosis (must be >5K; often >100K)]], frequently anemia; [[★ diagnosis confirmed by flow cytometry]] (clonal B-cell population); absolute lymphocyte count >5K for 3 months, or <5K with lymphadenopathy or other symptoms; coexpression of CD19 and CD5; cytogenetics for prognosis; bone marrow biopsy usually not required. Rai stage (0 asymptomatic lymphocytosis; I + lymphadenopathy; II + organomegaly; III + anemia; IV + thrombocytopenia) from exam and labs. Differential: monoclonal B lymphocytosis (elevated count but <5K with no nodes, organomegaly, cytopenias or symptoms; progresses to chronic lymphocytic leukemia 1-2% per year), atypical lymphocytosis with infection (pertussis), Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia, hairy cell leukemia, lymphomas in leukemic phase
fields.treatment: [[★ Watch and wait]] if asymptomatic until rapid progression (lymphocyte count doubling in <6 months) or disease-related symptoms. Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitors (ibrutinib, acalabrutinib, zanubrutinib), usually continuous as monotherapy; BCL-2 inhibitor venetoclax combined with monoclonal antibodies for a fixed duration; monoclonal antibodies (rituximab, obinutuzumab, ofatumumab); trend toward combinations. Referral to and management by hematology/oncology; unlikely to need hospitalization; pill therapy (once or twice daily, indefinite) or infusion + pill (time-limited, more intensive)
fields.mortality: 5-year relative survival ~88% (since 2013); [[★ risk of Richter transformation]] to an aggressive B-cell lymphoma with poor outcomes; many patients will die with chronic lymphocytic leukemia rather than from it; very good long-term prognosis likely

conditions.name: Non-Hodgkin lymphoma (the group)
conditions.prof_note: Said: on a test expect HIV, EBV, HTLV-1, H. pylori; excisional biopsy is the key (never trust a negative fine needle aspiration); LDH on every lymphoma; staging by the diaphragm; T cells always worse than B cells. Slide emphasis: 85% B-cell, >2/3 lymphadenopathy, B symptoms, CT or PET.

fields.name: Non-Hodgkin lymphoma (the group)
fields.definition: A [[★ diverse group of malignancies of lymphoid tissues derived from B cells, T cells, or NK cells]] that present frequently with lymphadenopathy; [[★ 85% B-cell]], 15% T-cell or NK-cell; ranges from very aggressive (Burkitt, diffuse large B-cell, T-cell leukemia/lymphoma) to indolent (follicular, marginal zone, chronic lymphocytic leukemia/small lymphocytic lymphoma)
fields.etiology: Immunosuppression, autoimmunity, chronic infection and environmental exposure (the risk factor list); subtype-defining genes: t(14;18) BCL-2 (follicular), cyclin D1 t(11;14) (mantle cell), MYC (Burkitt), MYD88 (lymphoplasmacytic)
fields.epidemiology: 4% of all new cancer diagnoses in the United States; higher incidence in White individuals and developed countries; male gender
fields.risk_factors: Male gender; immunosuppression (prior immunotherapy, chemotherapy, radiation, malignancy; prior transplantation); autoimmune conditions (lupus, Sjogren, celiac); Crohn's; environmental exposures including DDT (farming); chronic infections: H. pylori gastritis (MALT), HTLV-1, hepatitis C, HIV, Epstein-Barr virus, Lyme disease, HHV-8; family history
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: [[★ Peripheral lymphadenopathy in >2/3]]; [[★ B symptoms (weight loss, night sweats, fever of unknown origin)]], rash, hypersensitivity reactions, fatigue, pruritus, malaise, ascites, effusion; about half develop extranodal disease; CNS lymphoma: headaches, lethargy, neurologic defects; primary mediastinal B-cell lymphoma: large mediastinal mass, cough, abnormal chest X-ray
fields.diagnosis: [[★ Excisional lymph node biopsy]] for significant enlargement (2 cm), persistent, progressive; avoid fine needle aspiration (architecture needed; may miss the diagnosis); [[★ imaging (usually CT or PET) to characterize and stage]]; complete blood count (cytopenias with marrow involvement), chemistries (electrolytes, rule out tumor lysis syndrome), LDH (rapid proliferation); bone marrow biopsy; lumbar puncture for high-grade lymphomas including Burkitt. Lugano staging (modified Ann Arbor): 1 single node region or organ; 2 two or more regions same side of the diaphragm; 3 above and below the diaphragm; 4 widespread, multiple organs
fields.treatment: Highly dependent on subtype: single node, non-aggressive: radiation; low-grade B-cell: rituximab (anti-CD20) if treatment required +/- chemotherapy if extensive; aggressive B-cell: multi-drug chemotherapy such as R-CHOP (rituximab, cyclophosphamide, vincristine, doxorubicin, prednisone); T-cell: CHOP minus rituximab (no CD20 on T cells). Hematologist referral, ideally a lymphoma expert; hospitalization for aggressive disease with electrolyte abnormalities, otherwise outpatient; drink plenty of fluids and take allopurinol on starting treatment
fields.mortality: [[★ Tumor lysis syndrome]] (medical emergency); infections, bleeding, anemia, electrolyte abnormalities, diarrhea with all chemotherapy. Indolent lymphomas incurable but survival often 10-15+ years, with risk of progression to aggressive lymphoma; aggressive lymphomas often treatable and curable with chemotherapy, 5-year survival 60-70% (the slide's cure percentage was corrected out loud upward, to about 70%); T-cell respond less well than B-cell. Poor prognosis: age >60, extranodal sites, ECOG performance status >2, stage III or IV, elevated LDH

conditions.name: Follicular lymphoma
conditions.prof_note: Said of t(14;18) and BCL-2: "You probably don't need to know this."

fields.name: Follicular lymphoma
fields.definition: The most common indolent histology of non-Hodgkin lymphoma
fields.etiology: Chromosomal translocation t(14;18) places the BCL-2 gene on chromosome 14, preventing cell death
fields.epidemiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.risk_factors: Not covered in the lecture
fields.pathology: Microscopy often shows clusters of packed follicles
fields.clinical: Typically indolent: waxing and waning painless lymphadenopathy
fields.diagnosis: Microscopy: clusters of packed follicles; excisional biopsy and staging as for non-Hodgkin lymphoma
fields.treatment: Frequently no treatment required (watch and wait); intermittent low-intensity therapy if symptomatic; high-risk follicular lymphoma may need more aggressive chemotherapies and immunotherapies
fields.mortality: Often no treatment or only intermittent treatment, but incurable; indolent lymphomas survive often 10-15+ years with risk of progression to aggressive lymphoma

conditions.name: Marginal zone lymphoma (including MALT lymphoma)
conditions.prof_note: Said: gastric MALT with H. pylori "you may want to know that"; nodal and splenic subtypes "you probably won't be asked that".

fields.name: Marginal zone lymphoma (including MALT lymphoma)
fields.definition: Indolent non-Hodgkin lymphomas, 5-17% of all non-Hodgkin lymphoma, most commonly the extranodal subtype; subtypes: extranodal or mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT, most common), nodal marginal zone, splenic marginal zone
fields.etiology: Gastric MALT: 2/3 of cases associated with H. pylori; splenic marginal zone associated with hepatitis C
fields.epidemiology: 5-17% of non-Hodgkin lymphoma; more common in older adults
fields.risk_factors: H. pylori gastritis; hepatitis C; older age
fields.pathology: MALT involves organs with mucosa: gastrointestinal tract, eyes, lungs
fields.clinical: Not covered in the lecture
fields.diagnosis: Not covered in the lecture
fields.treatment: Not covered in the lecture
fields.mortality: Indolent lymphomas: incurable but survival often 10-15+ years

conditions.name: Lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma (Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia)
conditions.prof_note: Said: farming, pesticides - "kind of always choose that on the test if you see it".

fields.name: Lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma (Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia)
fields.definition: An indolent lymphoma, also known as Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia, affecting lymphoplasmacytoid cells and plasma cells (terminally differentiated B cells)
fields.etiology: MYD88 mutation frequently found (~90% of cases)
fields.epidemiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.risk_factors: Genetic (familial); environmental (farming, pesticides)
fields.pathology: Excess IgM production: a large antibody that causes hyperviscosity
fields.clinical: Hyperviscosity: blurred vision, headache, rarely stroke (cerebrovascular accident)
fields.diagnosis: MYD88 mutation; IgM monoclonal protein (different pathophysiology and treatment from myeloma)
fields.treatment: Not covered in the lecture
fields.mortality: Good prognosis overall; relative 5-year survival 78%

conditions.name: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
conditions.prof_note: Said: the slide's 50% cure is too low, "more closely to 70%"; stage matters less for treatment because it behaves aggressively.

fields.name: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
fields.definition: An aggressive B-cell lymphoma, the most common non-Hodgkin lymphoma in adults, with many subtypes by location, mutations and infectious associations
fields.etiology: Many subtypes based on location, mutations, and infectious associations
fields.epidemiology: Most common non-Hodgkin lymphoma in adults
fields.risk_factors: Older age, family history, autoimmune conditions, infections, environmental
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Fast-growing mass/swelling and/or B symptoms (fever, fatigue, night sweats, weight loss)
fields.diagnosis: Excisional biopsy, CT or PET staging and labs as for non-Hodgkin lymphoma
fields.treatment: Aggressive B-cell lymphoma: multi-drug chemotherapy such as R-CHOP (rituximab, cyclophosphamide, vincristine, doxorubicin, prednisone)
fields.mortality: Often treatable and curable with multi-agent chemotherapy (slide 34 prints a cure percentage that she corrected out loud: "more closely to 70%"); aggressive lymphomas: 5-year survival 60-70%; tumor lysis syndrome risk

conditions.name: Mantle cell lymphoma
conditions.prof_note: Said: "pretty rare, I'm surprised it's even on here".

fields.name: Mantle cell lymphoma
fields.definition: A rare subtype of non-Hodgkin lymphoma identified by the cyclin D1 gene translocation t(11;14); typically aggressive, though an indolent variant has been described
fields.etiology: Cyclin D1 gene translocation t(11;14)
fields.epidemiology: 5% of all non-Hodgkin lymphoma; more common in men; median age 60-70 years
fields.risk_factors: Male sex; age 60-70
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Not covered in the lecture
fields.diagnosis: Cyclin D1 translocation t(11;14)
fields.treatment: Not covered in the lecture
fields.mortality: Median survival from under 2 years to over 9, depending on the aggressive or indolent variant

conditions.name: T-cell lymphomas, including cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (mycosis fungoides, Sezary syndrome)
conditions.prof_note: Said: T cells behave more aggressively than B cells; HTLV-1 "you should know".

fields.name: T-cell lymphomas, including cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (mycosis fungoides, Sezary syndrome)
fields.definition: A diverse group of non-Hodgkin lymphomas with many subtypes: peripheral T-cell lymphoma, not otherwise specified (most common, 1/3), nodal T-cell, anaplastic large cell (aggressive), adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (very aggressive), intestinal, extranodal NK/T-cell (often nasal), hepatosplenic; cutaneous T-cell lymphoma = mycosis fungoides, with a more aggressive form, Sezary syndrome
fields.etiology: Adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma is associated with HTLV-1
fields.epidemiology: 15% of non-Hodgkin lymphoma are T-cell or NK-cell; adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma more common in the Caribbean, Central and South America
fields.risk_factors: HTLV-1 infection
fields.pathology: Mycosis fungoides often has no visceral involvement
fields.clinical: Mycosis fungoides: skin lesions that resemble fungal infections, progressing to nodular lesions that may ulcerate; Sezary syndrome: widespread, red, itchy rash (erythroderma) with severe pruritus and diminished quality of life; extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma often affects the nasal region
fields.diagnosis: Not covered in the lecture
fields.treatment: T-cell lymphomas: CHOP-type regimens minus rituximab (no CD20 expression on T cells); cutaneous T-cell lymphoma: treatment focused on the skin manifestations
fields.mortality: T-cell lymphomas respond less well than B-cell lymphomas; adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma very aggressive

conditions.name: Burkitt lymphoma
conditions.prof_note: Said: "If a pathologist ever says starry sky, you think Burkitt's ... you'll definitely see that on a test"; endemic region sub-Saharan Africa, strongly associated with EBV. Slide emphasis: prompt treatment with emergent referral; tumor lysis.

fields.name: Burkitt lymphoma
fields.definition: A very aggressive lymphoma variant with three types: endemic, sporadic, immunodeficiency-associated
fields.etiology: Associated with MYC gene upregulation, resulting in stimulated cell growth and division; endemic type strongly associated with Epstein-Barr virus; immunodeficiency type associated with HIV/AIDS
fields.epidemiology: Endemic: largely sub-Saharan Africa and New Guinea; sporadic: United States and Western Europe, more in males, almost always under age 35; immunodeficiency-associated: HIV/AIDS
fields.risk_factors: Epstein-Barr virus (endemic); HIV/AIDS; male sex and age under 35 (sporadic)
fields.pathology: [[★ "Starry sky" appearance]]: sheets of lymphoma with benign macrophages clearing out dying lymphoma cells; extremely fast doubling time
fields.clinical: Very rapidly growing, often painless swelling (visible change within one day); commonly B symptoms (fever, night sweats, weight loss)
fields.diagnosis: Pathology: starry sky; high-grade lymphomas including Burkitt require a lumbar puncture
fields.treatment: [[★ Prompt treatment with emergent referral to a hematologist]]; rapid transfer of care; multi-agent chemotherapy; caution starting therapy because of tumor lysis syndrome
fields.mortality: Excellent long-term prognosis if identified and treated early: >90% in children, 50-90% in adults; [[★ tumor lysis syndrome]], which can occur spontaneously

conditions.name: Hodgkin lymphoma
conditions.prof_note: Said: Reed-Sternberg cells - "automatically think of Hodgkin's"; ABVD + painless lymphadenopathy = Hodgkin; node pain after alcohol as a test clue. Slide emphasis: bimodal, EBV 40-50%, painless cervical nodes, >90% alive at 5 years.

fields.name: Hodgkin lymphoma
fields.definition: A type of B-cell lymphoma characterized by few malignant cells ([[★ Reed-Sternberg cells]]: binucleated, neoplastic B cells) among numerous immune effector cells; contiguous, orderly spread through lymph nodes
fields.etiology: Epstein-Barr virus suspected (identified in 40-50% of cases); others including HIV, HHV-6, tuberculosis
fields.epidemiology: ~10-15% of all lymphoma diagnoses worldwide; [[★ bimodal incidence]]: adults in their 20s and adults >60
fields.risk_factors: Same-sex siblings have a 10x increased risk; [[★ Epstein-Barr virus (40-50%)]]; HIV, HHV-6, tuberculosis
fields.pathology: Reed-Sternberg cells; classical Hodgkin lymphoma expresses CD15 and CD30; spreads contiguously
fields.clinical: [[★ Painless asymptomatic lymphadenopathy (70%)]], [[★ usually cervical]], could be supraclavicular or mediastinal; [[★ pain may worsen with alcohol consumption]]; mediastinal mass on chest X-ray; splenomegaly (~30%), sometimes hepatomegaly; pruritus, may be very intense
fields.diagnosis: Excisional lymph node biopsy (avoid fine needle aspiration); classical type CD15 and CD30; chest X-ray rules out mediastinal mass/adenopathy; complete blood count, chemistries (rule out tumor lysis), LDH; bone marrow biopsy; Lugano staging (modified Ann Arbor)
fields.treatment: Early stage I and IIA: short course of chemotherapy ([[★ ABVD]] historically); bulky stage I or II or B symptoms: chemotherapy + radiation; stage III or IV: chemotherapy. ABVD: doxorubicin (Adriamycin), bleomycin, vinblastine, dacarbazine; new agents replacing bleomycin because of pulmonary toxicities. Relapse after first line: allogeneic stem cell transplant
fields.mortality: [[★ Generally curable, >90% alive at 5 years]]; inferior results with older patients, bulky disease, lymphocyte-depleted or mixed-cellularity subtypes; delayed toxicities: myelodysplastic syndrome, secondary leukemia, other cancers

conditions.name: Multiple myeloma
conditions.prof_note: Said: CRAB - "it will 100% be on a test in some form"; myeloma needs only 10% marrow plasma cells (vs 20% blasts in acute leukemia); remember Bence Jones protein; "we don't use staging too much in myeloma". Slide emphasis: diagnosis line, 3- or 4-drug regimen, most relapse, incurable.

fields.name: Multiple myeloma
fields.definition: A malignant, incurable clonal disorder of plasma cells (terminally differentiated B cells), at the far end of the plasma cell disorder spectrum from MGUS
fields.etiology: Clonal evolution of plasma cells produces a single, overproduced antibody type, most commonly IgG
fields.epidemiology: 10% of all hematologic malignancies; most diagnoses over age 65; African Americans at higher risk
fields.risk_factors: Age (most over 65); African American race; family history; prior MGUS or smoldering myeloma; environmental exposures (radiation, chemical, occupational)
fields.pathology: Activates osteoclasts, releasing calcium into the bloodstream; renal dysfunction from light chain and calcium phosphate deposition; anemia from renal dysfunction and marrow involvement; osteolytic "punched out" lesions
fields.clinical: [[★ CRAB]]: calcium (hypercalcemia: constipation, increased thirst, urinary frequency, nausea); renal insufficiency (swelling); anemia (fatigue, shortness of breath); bone lesions/pain (back, chest, pelvis). May be asymptomatic with certain lab findings (SLiM: bone marrow plasma cells >=60%, light chain ratio >100:1, MRI >=2 lesions). Higher risk of infections; also amyloidosis, hyperviscosity, polyneuropathies
fields.diagnosis: [[★ >=10% bone marrow plasma cells or biopsy-proven plasmacytoma + 1 or more CRAB feature]]; monoclonal protein on serum protein electrophoresis is characteristic; urine [[★ Bence Jones protein]]; complete blood count, metabolic/electrolyte panel, 24-hour urine protein electrophoresis, bone marrow biopsy with flow, kappa/lambda light chain ratio, beta-2 microglobulin, whole-body CT for bone lesions. R-ISS: I beta-2 microglobulin <3.5 mg/L, albumin >=3.5 g/dL, standard-risk chromosomes, normal LDH; II not I or III; III beta-2 microglobulin >=5.5 mg/L, high-risk chromosomes (del 17p, t(4;14), t(14;16)), high LDH; prognostic only. Differential: smoldering myeloma, MGUS, Waldenstrom (IgM), chronic lymphocytic leukemia, non-Hodgkin lymphoma, amyloidosis, reactive hypergammaglobulinemia (cirrhosis, chronic inflammation)
fields.treatment: [[★ Goal: prolonged remissions to improve survival and quality of life]]; [[★ newly diagnosed: 3- or 4-drug regimen]] with a proteasome inhibitor and immunomodulatory drug backbone with steroids; autologous transplant (and maintenance after) if a candidate; continuous therapy at relapse; CAR-T, bispecifics, antibody-drug conjugates for relapsed myeloma. Hematologist/oncologist, ideally a myeloma expert; lifelong treatment and follow-up
fields.mortality: 5-year relative survival ~60% (2018-2022); [[★ each line of therapy has shorter remissions; incurable/fatal]]; [[★ most patients relapse]]; newly diagnosed patients today may survive >10 years

fields.name: Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS)
fields.definition: A clonal, low-level plasma cell disorder: M-protein <3 g/dL, clonal bone marrow plasma cells <10%, no myeloma-defining characteristics; by definition asymptomatic (the slide title says "unknown significance")
fields.etiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.epidemiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.risk_factors: Not covered in the lecture
fields.pathology: Clonal proliferation of plasma cells at a low level
fields.clinical: Asymptomatic by definition
fields.diagnosis: M-protein <3 g/dL; clonal bone marrow plasma cells <10%; no myeloma-defining characteristics
fields.treatment: Not covered in the lecture
fields.mortality: Risk of progression to myeloma ~1% per year; a risk factor for multiple myeloma

fields.name: Smoldering myeloma
fields.definition: An intermediate-stage clonal plasma cell disorder: M-protein >3 g/dL AND 10-60% bone marrow plasma cells, with no myeloma-defining events
fields.etiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.epidemiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.risk_factors: Not covered in the lecture
fields.pathology: Intermediate stage between MGUS and myeloma; a more indolent process
fields.clinical: No myeloma-defining events (anemia, bone lesions, renal failure, etc.); no symptoms
fields.diagnosis: M-protein >3 g/dL and 10-60% bone marrow plasma cells without anemia, bone lesions or renal failure
fields.treatment: Typically does not require treatment (often monitored); may consider early intervention for some subgroups
fields.mortality: [[★ Progression approximately 10% per year]]; some high-risk groups >50% risk of progression within 2 years; a risk factor for multiple myeloma

conditions.name: Tumor lysis syndrome
conditions.prof_note: Said: "Very important to know this ... an oncologic emergency. You need to know it, you need to recognize it for your testing"; high potassium, high phosphorus, high uric acid (she added low calcium, not on the slide); fluids and allopurinol.

fields.name: Tumor lysis syndrome
fields.definition: A [[★ medical emergency]] due to rapid tumor breakdown and release of cellular products (potassium, phosphorus, uric acid)
fields.etiology: Rapid tumor breakdown, spontaneously in highly aggressive lymphomas (Burkitt) or on starting therapy
fields.epidemiology: Aggressive lymphoma (Burkitt); also acute lymphoblastic and acute myeloid leukemia with marked leukocytosis
fields.risk_factors: Highly aggressive lymphoma; starting chemotherapy
fields.pathology: Release of potassium, phosphorus and uric acid; uric acid and calcium phosphate crystals precipitate in the renal tubules
fields.clinical: Arrhythmia from hyperkalemia; acute renal failure
fields.diagnosis: Chemistries (electrolytes) in the lymphoma work-up to rule it out
fields.treatment: [[★ Requires aggressive IV fluid hydration]]; anticipate in aggressive lymphoma: allopurinol (hypouricemic agent) and fluids in advance; patients drink plenty of fluids and take allopurinol
fields.mortality: Largest risk: hyperkalemia leading to arrhythmia and potential death; acute renal failure
